newsitem.title: USA: Chicago ruled immune from 1992 flood damage claims.
newsitem.headline: Chicago ruled immune from 1992 flood damage claims.

text.p: The Illinois Supreme Court has ruled that Chicago is not liable for $300 million in claims brought against it as a result of an April 1992 underground flood, the city's law department announced Thursday.

The 6 to 1 decision by the state's high court found that Chicago is immune against liability for any alleged negligence in supervising a dredging firm that drove a piling into a tunnel beneath the Chicago River flooding downtown basements with more than 250 million gallons of water.
The court also ruled the city was immune from claims that it failed to repair the tunnel or to warn of tunnel damage.

"Tort immunity exists to protect the taxpayers, who should not have to fund enormous judgements because of the alleged negligence of a few municipal employees," said Susan Sher, the city's corporation counsel in a news release.
Chicago fired some city employees charged with overseeing work by Great Lakes Dredge & Dock Co in the aftermath of the flood.

The ruling came in a class-action case filed by downtown business owners and a separate lawsuit filed by ITT Hartford, an insurer that has paid claims related to the flood, the city's law department said.
A spokesperson for ITT Hartford and a Chicago attorney representing the class-action litigants were not immediately available to comment.
The state supreme court also ruled that only businesses whose own property was damaged by water had the right to recover damages. The court then sent the case back to trial court.
Sher said she doubted any of the claims in the lawsuit would survive given the court's ruling on the city's liability.
